title: Before You Ask Someone to Date You… Ask God This One Question First
paragraphs:
Before You Ask Someone to Date You… Ask God This One Question First
Is it really wrong to date if you don't have a job yet—or is the real issue something much deeper than money?
Some questions expose far more than they answer.
"Is it okay to date if I don't have a job yet?"
At first glance, it sounds like a financial question. But beneath it lives something far heavier.
Am I enough?
Will anyone want me if I cannot provide?
Am I failing as a man?
Am I wasting her time?
Should I wait until my life is perfect before I let someone love me?

Those questions have quietly haunted countless young believers. Some hide behind jokes. Others bury themselves in endless self-improvement. Some rush into relationships hoping love will heal insecurities that only Christ can touch. Others isolate themselves for years, believing they must earn the right to be loved.
Yet Scripture never tells us that employment determines our worth.
It tells us that Jesus does.
This is where the conversation must begin.
Long before discussing dating, careers, or marriage, the Bible introduces us to a God who has always looked deeper than outward success.
When the prophet Samuel was searching for Israel's next king, God corrected his perspective:
"Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart." (1 Samuel 16:7)
The Hebrew word translated "heart" is לֵב (lev).
It does not merely refer to emotions.
It means the center of one's character, intentions, mind, convictions, and will.
God evaluates the lev before He evaluates achievements.
That alone should reshape the entire conversation.
Having no job does not automatically make someone unfit for dating.
But having no direction, no responsibility, no teachable spirit, and no desire to honor God—that is another matter entirely.
Many people assume financial stability is the biblical requirement for a relationship.
Interestingly, Scripture never says that.
Instead, Scripture repeatedly emphasizes diligence.
Paul writes:
Notice the wording carefully.
Paul does not condemn someone who cannot find work.
He addresses someone who is not willing to work.
The Greek phrase is οὐ θέλει ἐργάζεσθαι (ou thelei ergazesthai).
It literally means "does not desire to work."
This is a heart issue.
Not an economic one.
God understands unemployment.
He understands recessions.
He understands layoffs.
He understands graduates still searching.
He understands sickness.
He understands seasons.
But Scripture consistently calls believers toward faithful stewardship, not passive entitlement.
Dating is similar.
The question is not merely:
"Do you have a paycheck?"
The better question is:
"Are you becoming the kind of person who reflects Christ?"
Because eventually every relationship will encounter financial hardship.
Jobs disappear.
Businesses fail.
Economies collapse.
Health changes.
Dreams shift.
If a relationship is built only upon income, it will eventually collapse under pressure.
If it is built upon Christ, it has something deeper than money holding it together.
Jesus Himself never chose His disciples based on wealth.
Several had unstable occupations.
Matthew had a controversial career.
Peter owned fishing equipment but still experienced seasons where he caught nothing.
Others left everything immediately.
None were selected because they possessed financial perfection.
They were chosen because Christ was transforming them.
That transformation remains God's highest priority today.
However, this should never become an excuse for laziness.
Love is not merely romance.
Biblical love always carries responsibility.
Paul writes:
Real love asks:
How can I serve?
How can I protect?
How can I encourage?
How can I sacrifice?
Dating should prepare two believers to answer those questions together.
Marriage magnifies them.
This is why Proverbs repeatedly celebrates diligence.
"Go to the ant, O sluggard..."
The Hebrew word for sluggard is עָצֵל ('atsel).
It describes someone habitually lazy, unwilling to act despite opportunity.
Scripture does not condemn temporary unemployment.
It warns against habitual irresponsibility.
There is a profound difference.

Someone actively seeking work, growing in wisdom, serving their church, helping their family, managing their finances wisely, and pursuing Christ may be far more prepared for a relationship than someone earning a large salary while living selfishly.
Income impresses people.
Character sustains covenant.
That distinction matters immensely.
The modern world often tells young men that their value begins with six figures.
The Gospel says your value began at Calvary.
Your paycheck did not purchase your soul.
Jesus did.
Peter reminds believers:
"You were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ." (1 Peter 1:18–19)
No salary can increase your worth before God.
Likewise, no unemployment can erase it.
Still, wisdom asks honest questions before pursuing someone.
Can you lead her toward Christ?
Can you pray with her?
Can you encourage holiness?
Can you practice self-control?
Can you communicate honestly?
Can you accept correction?
Can you work diligently toward your responsibilities?
Those questions often reveal more about readiness than a job title.
Dating should never become an escape from adulthood.
Nor should adulthood become an excuse to delay obedience forever.
Some postpone relationships endlessly until every financial goal has been achieved.
Ironically, life rarely becomes perfectly stable.
There will always be another promotion.
Another investment.
Another milestone.
Another reason to wait.
Waiting for perfection often becomes fear wearing the mask of wisdom.
On the other hand, rushing into dating because of loneliness is equally dangerous.
Loneliness makes poor counselors.
Christ must remain sufficient before another person becomes significant.
Otherwise, we ask relationships to carry burdens only Jesus can bear.
The Apostle Paul repeatedly grounds every area of life in Christ first.
Identity precedes activity.
Grace precedes growth.
Redemption precedes responsibility.
That is the rhythm of the Gospel.
Not performance first.
Grace first.
This is exactly why our ministry says:
Many believers carry the scandal of unemployment.
Others carry the scandal of failure.
Rejected applications.
Closed businesses.
Debt.
Family expectations.
Embarrassment.
Comparison.
Silent shame.
The world writes people off because of resumes.
Jesus rewrites people because of redemption.
The greatest scandal in history was not unemployment.
It was the cross.
Yet what looked like ultimate defeat became eternal victory.
Grace rewrote everything.
Perhaps today you have no job.
Perhaps you feel invisible.
Perhaps you believe no one could ever respect you until your career is established.
Hear this carefully.
Your future spouse should never become your savior.
Your career should never become your identity.
Your income should never become your righteousness.
Only Christ deserves those places.
Seek work diligently.
Grow faithfully.
Develop wisdom.
Honor your parents if you are under their care.
Serve your local church.
Build integrity.
Manage whatever resources God has already entrusted to you.
Become the kind of disciple someone else could safely walk beside.
Then trust God's timing.
The Gospel has never promised instant success.
It promises faithful transformation.
Jesus did not die merely to improve your circumstances.
He died to make you new.
That changes everything.
If this message challenged or encouraged you, don't let it end with you. They may need this reminder today more than you realize.

Your support allows this ministry to continue creating biblically faithful content that points people from scandal to grace, equips believers for discipleship, and reaches those who have yet to hear the hope of the Gospel.
Because someone else's eternity may begin with a post you were willing to share today.
